# African networks: sources and route notes

Research checked September 21, 2026. Story copy is in `tour-stories.md`; the geographic route data is in `tour-africa.mjs`.

## Reading the map

Five periods show selected networks around 200, 950, 1300, 1480 and 1750 CE. Routes join known towns, mines, ports and oases with schematic corridors; they are not caravan itineraries and carry no estimate of volume. Enslaved people are drawn as a wave of their own, in red, so that the trade in people is named rather than folded into "goods". Lines marked uncertain rest on archaeology or later sources rather than contemporary records.

## Sahara and Sahel

- [Britannica: Garamantes](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Garamantes). A Fezzan-based people trading with Roman Tripolitania and, by inference from wells, imports and burials, southward toward the Sahel. The southern link is drawn fainter.
- [Britannica: trans-Saharan trade](https://www.britannica.com/topic/trans-Saharan-trade) and [UNESCO: Timbuktu](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/119/). Camel caravans carried Saharan salt (Taghaza), Maghribi cloth, copper and horses south and gold, ivory and captives north, through Sijilmasa, Walata, Timbuktu, Gao and the Fezzan. Ghana, Mali and Songhai in turn controlled the southern ends.
- [Britannica: Mali empire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mali-historical-empire) and [Britannica: Songhai empire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Songhai-empire). Context for the 1300 and 1480 chapters. Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Cairo is treated as evidence for the Sahel–Cairo corridor, not drawn as a journey.
- [Britannica: Kanem-Bornu](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kanem-Bornu). The Lake Chad route to Tripoli through the Fezzan carried captives north for centuries.

## Nile, Red Sea and the Horn

- [UNESCO: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1336/) and [UNESCO: Aksum](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/15/). Meroë traded gold, ivory and iron with Roman Egypt; Aksum exported ivory through Adulis and traded with South Arabia, as the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes.
- The Nubia–Cairo and Ethiopia–Red Sea captive routes are documented in medieval Arabic sources summarized in the Britannica entries above; their drawn corridors follow the Nile and the caravan tracks to Zeila.

## Swahili coast and the interior

- [UNESCO: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/144/), [UNESCO: Great Zimbabwe National Monument](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/364/) and [UNESCO: Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1099/). Kilwa controlled the Sofala gold trade from the Zimbabwe plateau in the 13th–15th centuries; Mapungubwe's earlier gold and glass beads show the same coast–interior link, drawn fainter for 950.
- Monsoon trade between the Swahili towns, the Persian Gulf, Aden and Gujarat carried ivory, gold and enslaved people east and cloth, beads and ceramics west ([Britannica: Swahili coast](https://www.britannica.com/place/Swahili-coast)).

## Atlantic

- [Slave Voyages: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database](https://www.slavevoyages.org/). The regional lanes (Senegambia, Gold Coast, Bights of Benin and Biafra, West Central Africa, Southeast Africa) and destinations (Caribbean, Brazil, North America) follow the database's regions; the figure of about 12.5 million embarked is its estimate for the whole trade. Individual ship tracks are not drawn.
- [UNESCO: Forts and Castles of Ghana](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/) and [Britannica: Kongo](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kongo-historical-kingdom). Elmina (1482) began the Portuguese gold trade; Kongo and São Tomé the Atlantic trade in captives. Benin's cloth and pepper trade and the Senegambia–Arguin route are drawn fainter.
- Interior routes (Kazembe–Luanda, Sahel–Senegambia) are known from later accounts and are drawn as uncertain.

## Deliberate limits

No volumes are shown. West African river trade, the Ethiopian highlands, the Great Lakes, the Indian Ocean island networks and many regional systems are omitted. Modern coastlines and country borders are not implied; the hexagonal map's cuts interrupt lines without implying interrupted trade.
